There is a concept in the Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows called *sonder*: the realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own. I want to apply that concept not to people, but to time. Specifically, to the "unrecorded history" of the mundane.

History books are obsessed with peaks and valleys. They record the treaties signed, the volcanoes that erupted, the empires that fell, and the inventions that changed the trajectory of the species. History is a highlight reel of human trauma and triumph. 

Because of this, it is easy to look back at the past as a series of dramatic, sepia-toned tableaux. We imagine the Romans constantly debating in the Senate or fighting in the Colosseum. We imagine the 1920s as an endless loop of jazz and flapper dresses, or the Middle Ages as a relentless slog of plague and swordplay.

What gets entirely erased is the connective tissue of existence: the Tuesdays. 

I find myself infinitely fascinated by the billions of ordinary, unremarkable afternoons that have vanished into the ether. 

Think about a rainy afternoon in a Mesopotamian village, four thousand years ago. Nothing of historical note happened that day. The king didn't die; no laws were carved into stone. Instead, a potter sat under an awning, annoyed that the humidity was keeping his clay from drying properly. Maybe his lower back hurt. Maybe he was smelling the stew his neighbor was cooking—something heavy with onions and coriander—and thinking about how he needed to fix a leak in his roof before the heavy rains came. 

He felt the chill in the air just as acutely as you feel the temperature in the room you are sitting in right now. The boredom, the minor irritation, the sensory reality of the wet mud between his fingers—it was all 100% real, occupying the entirety of the present moment. And then the day ended, and nobody wrote it down, and everyone who remembered it eventually turned to dust.

Or think about the jokes. Humor is so ephemeral. For tens of thousands of years, humans have been sitting around fires, tables, and taverns, making each other laugh until their stomachs hurt. Imagine a group of builders taking a lunch break in the shadow of the half-finished Notre-Dame cathedral in the year 1200. One of them says something so blisteringly funny, some specific roast of the foreman or a clever observation about a stray dog, that the others nearly choke on their bread. That moment of pure, golden human joy existed. It echoed off the stone. And then it evaporated. We have the cathedral, the grand monument of their labor, standing in Paris today. We can touch the stone. But the joke—which was arguably the best part of their day—is gone forever.

I think about the forgotten errands. The medieval peasant walking three miles just to return a borrowed iron pot. The Victorian clerk spending twenty minutes looking for a misplaced spectacle case before realizing it was in his coat pocket the whole time. The teenager in 1974 staring at the ceiling, waiting for a phone call that never came, listening to the hum of the refrigerator.

There is something deeply comforting about the weight of all this forgotten mundanity. 

In our modern era, we are terrified of being forgotten, and we are terrified of being ordinary. We document everything—our meals, our outfits, our fleeting thoughts—trying to fossilize our daily lives into something permanent, something "historic." We feel a constant pressure to be exceptional, to leave a mark.

But when you zoom out and realize that 99.9% of the human experience has been made up of unrecorded, quiet, ordinary moments, the pressure lifts. 

Right now, you are reading these words. Maybe you are procrastinating on something. Maybe you are drinking coffee that has gone slightly lukewarm, or maybe you are lying in bed at night, the screen illuminating your face. This moment will not make it into the history books. In a hundred years, no one will know that you were sitting right here, right now, breathing in and out. 

And that is entirely okay. In fact, it’s wonderful. You are participating in the grandest, longest-running tradition in the universe: just being alive on an ordinary day, keeping the world spinning between the pages of the history books.
